title: Rim Joist / Band Joist Spray Foam Insulation
metaTitle: Rim Joist & Band Joist Spray Foam Insulation | St. George, UT
metaDescription: Seal the rim joist band at your foundation perimeter with closed-cell spray foam. Stop hot-air infiltration and monsoon dust in Washington County homes. Call 844-967-5247.
summary: Closed-cell spray foam applied directly to the rim joist / band joist cavity — the narrow strip of framing where your foundation meets your floor system — closing off one of the most overlooked air-leak points in any St. George home.
intro: If you've ever crawled under your house on a July afternoon and felt a wall of hot, dusty air pouring in around the edge of the foundation, you've met the rim joist. Also called the band joist, this is the narrow ribbon of framing that sits directly on top of your foundation wall, running the entire perimeter of your home and forming the outer edge of every floor system above a crawl space or basement. It's where the wood framing of your house meets the concrete or block of your foundation — and in most homes built in Washington County, that seam was never properly sealed in the first place.

Builders typically leave this cavity insulated with a thin batt of fiberglass stapled or friction-fit between the joists, if it's insulated at all. Fiberglass batts don't stop air movement — they only slow heat conduction — so the rim joist band stays one of the leakiest, most drafty sections of the entire building envelope. In a hot desert climate like ours, that means two things happen at once: superheated air from outside the crawl space or exterior wall cavity gets pulled in through every gap, and during monsoon season, wind-driven dust and fine debris rides right along with it, settling into ductwork, crawl spaces, and stored belongings.

Sealing the rim joist with closed-cell spray foam solves both problems in a single application. The foam expands to fill every irregular gap between the joists, sill plate, and foundation — sealing around plumbing penetrations, wiring runs, and the uneven lumber cuts that batts can never conform to — and it stays sealed permanently, with no settling, sagging, or gapping over time.

This is one of the fastest, most cost-effective upgrades we install. Because the rim joist band is a short, defined run of cavities rather than an entire attic or crawl space, most jobs take a fraction of the time of a full attic or crawl space project — which is exactly why we build it as a standard add-on whenever we're already on-site for an attic or crawl space job. If our crew is already mobilized at your property, sealing the rim joist band while we're there is the single best dollar-for-dollar upgrade available, because the setup and travel cost is already covered by the primary job.

As always, this is the only thing we do. We're not a general insulation company that also does spray foam — spray foam is the only thing we do, which is why we do it better than anyone else in Washington County. Every rim joist job we run uses the same closed-cell material and application standards as our flagship attic and roof-deck work, applied by the same crew, with no subcontracted batt-and-caulk shortcuts.

sections.heading: Why the Rim Joist Is a Chronic Air-Leak Point
body: The rim joist sits at a structural transition — foundation to framing — where multiple building trades meet: the foundation crew pours the wall, the framing crew sets the sill plate and joists, and the plumbing and electrical trades punch through with pipes and wire runs. Every one of those transitions creates a gap that's difficult to seal with conventional materials, and in practice, most of them never get sealed at all beyond a bead of caulk that shrinks and cracks within a few years.

Because the rim joist band runs the full perimeter of the house, even small gaps add up to a large total leak area — often rivaling or exceeding the air leakage from an unsealed attic hatch or an old exterior door. Energy auditors consistently flag the rim joist as one of the top three air-leak locations in a typical home, right alongside the attic and the areas around recessed lighting.
bullets: Sill plate to foundation wall gap, often visible as a continuous crack around the entire perimeter
Joist-to-joist gaps where batt insulation was friction-fit and has since settled or been disturbed
Plumbing and electrical penetrations that were never caulked or foamed after rough-in
Corner and transition framing where cavity shapes are irregular and standard batts can't conform

sections.heading: Stopping Hot-Air Infiltration in a Desert Climate
body: In St. George's climate, the rim joist doesn't just leak conditioned air out — it lets superheated, exterior-temperature air in, all summer long. With crawl space and exterior wall cavity temperatures climbing well above 100°F for weeks at a time between June and September, an unsealed rim joist band acts like a heat pipe running the entire perimeter of the house, feeding hot air directly into the floor system and up into interior wall cavities.

That infiltration works against your air conditioning system continuously, not just during the hottest part of the day. Because the leak path is passive and constant, it adds a steady, low-grade cooling load that doesn't show up as a single dramatic problem — it shows up as an AC system that runs longer than it should and utility bills that stay stubbornly high even after other upgrades. Sealing the rim joist band with closed-cell foam closes that path completely, which is why it pairs so well with attic sealing: together they address the two biggest passive heat-infiltration points in the home.

sections.heading: Blocking Monsoon Dust and Debris Infiltration
body: Washington County's monsoon season, running from mid/late July through early or mid-September, brings more than just humidity spikes and flash-flood risk — it brings sustained periods of wind-driven dust and fine debris. That dust doesn't stay outside. It finds every unsealed gap in the building envelope, and the rim joist band, with its continuous run of small, irregular openings around the entire foundation perimeter, is one of the primary entry points.

Once dust gets into the crawl space through the rim joist, it doesn't stay contained down there. Air pressure differences pull it up through floor penetrations, gaps around plumbing stacks, and any other opening between the crawl space and the living space above, where it ends up in HVAC returns, on interior surfaces, and in air filters that need changing far more often than they should. A properly sealed rim joist band stops that infiltration path at its source instead of trying to filter it out after the fact.

sections.heading: Why Closed-Cell Foam Is the Right Material for This Cavity
body: The rim joist band takes direct exposure to exterior temperature swings, occasional moisture from grade-level splash-back or monsoon runoff, and structural loads transferred from the foundation to the floor framing above. Closed-cell spray foam, at roughly R-6 to R-7 per inch, is the higher-density, higher-R-value option in our lineup, and it's the material we use for every rim joist job because it matches all three of those demands: it delivers strong R-value in a thin cavity, it adds rigid structural bracing to the joist bay, and its closed-cell structure resists moisture uptake far better than an open-cell product would in an exterior-adjacent assembly.

This is the same reasoning that guides our material choice on roof decks and other exterior-adjacent assemblies across every job we run — closed-cell where the cavity faces direct exterior exposure or takes a structural role, open-cell where the assembly is fully interior and moisture exposure isn't a factor.

faqs.q: What exactly is a rim joist or band joist?
faqs.a: It's the horizontal framing member that sits directly on top of your foundation wall, running around the entire perimeter of the house and forming the outer edge of your floor system. It's the transition point between the foundation and the wood framing above, and it's typically only accessible from inside a crawl space or basement.

faqs.q: Can you seal the rim joist without doing a full attic or crawl space job?
faqs.a: Yes. While it's most efficient as an add-on to an attic or crawl space project, we also run standalone rim joist jobs for homeowners who have a known dust, draft, or air-leak problem at the foundation perimeter and aren't ready for a larger project.

faqs.q: Will sealing the rim joist actually reduce dust in my house?
faqs.a: It addresses one of the primary entry points. If dust is getting into your crawl space through an unsealed rim joist band and then working its way up into the living space, sealing that seam closes off that specific infiltration path. It won't eliminate every source of household dust, but it removes a major contributor, especially during monsoon season.

faqs.q: Why not just use fiberglass batts in the rim joist cavity like most builders do?
faqs.a: Batts slow heat conduction but do nothing to stop air movement, and the irregular shape of rim joist cavities — with plumbing penetrations, wiring, and uneven lumber — means batts rarely fit tightly enough to make real contact with the framing. Closed-cell spray foam expands to fill every gap and seals the air leak completely, which is the actual problem in this cavity.

faqs.q: How long does a rim joist sealing job take?
faqs.a: As a standalone job, most homes are completed in a matter of hours, since the rim joist band is a short, defined run of cavities rather than an entire attic or crawl space. When it's bundled with a larger attic or crawl space job, it typically adds only a modest amount of time to the overall visit.
